The thing I have to explain to almost every adult learner at some point is that the feeling of progress and the fact of progress are two different measurements, and they do not move together. What happens is this. In the first months you improve and you feel it, because the things you fix are visible. Then you get past the obvious problems and the improvement continues, but it becomes invisible to you, because what is improving now is speed of retrieval, or recovery after a mistake, and nobody experiences those from the inside. Meanwhile your standard rises. Every week you notice things you would not have noticed a month ago, so you feel worse while performing better. This is the point where people conclude they have plateaued and stop, and they are almost always wrong. The answer is not to try harder. It is to measure something specific and compare it with a baseline, because feeling is a terrible instrument and a stopwatch is a very good one.

Deliberate practice is a phrase people use loosely, so let me be precise about what it actually means, because it is not the same as practising more. It means isolating the part you are worst at and repeating only that, under conditions slightly harder than the real thing, with feedback that arrives immediately. A pianist does not play the whole piece again. They play the four bars that break, forty times, slowly, then at speed. For somebody preparing for interviews in a second language, the equivalent is not having more conversations. It is taking the four seconds after a hard question, and doing only those four seconds, twenty times, with somebody who tells you at once what happened. It is boring, it is uncomfortable, and it is roughly ten times more efficient than a pleasant hour of general conversation.
